extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of mythology, folklore, and anthropology
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles for analyzing the origin, meaning, and development of myths, surveying competing schools (philological, anthropological, euhemerist, allegorical, etc.) and methodological cautions. Aimed at guiding scholarly treatment of mythic material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chronological and critical review of theories
rubrics_metrics.description: It will greatly assist comprehension to examine hypotheses and systems chronologically as well as critically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin with early thinkers and advance through the centuries to present-day theories so as to avoid pitfalls of earlier writers and errors caused by scarce data; survey historical development to evaluate contemporary views in context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain a myth by identifying its origin
rubrics_metrics.description: The explanation of a myth must be the explanation of its origin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretations should aim to trace how a myth arose (its original elements and causes), not only describe its later manifestations; resolve mythic materials into their original elements where possible (K.O. Müller).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish original myth from later poetic or philosophical sophistication
rubrics_metrics.description: Draw a distinction between the actual, original myth and the myth as sophisticated by poets and philosophers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separate layers: identify later literary, philosophical, or poetic accretions that have altered or obscured the primitive form; avoid treating sophisticated literary variants as if they represent primitive belief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use philology/linguistic evidence but not exclusively
rubrics_metrics.description: Mythology is to be comprehended principally through language, but not through language only; language may explain many but not all mythic phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply comparative philology and etymology to shed light on names and terms (e.g., Diaush-Pitar = Zeus Pater) but avoid overreliance—linguistic parallels can mislead when meanings have shifted or when similar myths occur in unrelated languages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of etymological overreach (etymology fallacy)
rubrics_metrics.description: The original meaning of a word is often totally at variance with its later use; etymological methods were often pushed to extremes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume that recovering an old lexical meaning automatically explains the entire myth; be cautious of conjectural or conflicting etymologies and of treating verbal derivations as sole explanatory causes (anti-pattern: treating 'a disease of language' as a universal solvent).

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare myths across widely divergent peoples
rubrics_metrics.description: The comparison of similar myths among widely divergent peoples frequently illuminates their primitive character and meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use cross-cultural comparison (including non-Indo-European and 'savage' societies) to test hypotheses; identical facts across different linguistic families suggest explanations not dependent on a single language-family's history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin study with low/primitive cultures to find origins (importance of savage myth)
rubrics_metrics.description: Savage mythology may be taken as a basis; the study should commence among races of low culture as they show rudimentary mythic conceptions most clearly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate myths and customs of less-advanced societies as they may preserve primitive forms; treat such material as a starting point for tracing evolutionary development of myths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat 'survivals' (primitive elements) as explanatory candidates
rubrics_metrics.description: The savage and irrational element in 'civilized' myth is composed of primitive survivals in more civilized times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for survivals of animism, fetishism, totemism, and other primitive beliefs embedded in later myths; consider ritual and folk-practice evidence for survivals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Group large numbers of myths to detect regularity and law
rubrics_metrics.description: The treatment of similar myths from different regions, by arranging them in large compared groups, makes it possible to trace in mythology the operation of imaginative processes recurring with the evident regularity of mental law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify and assemble broad comparative corpora; patterns emerging from many instances are more persuasive than isolated analogies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use circumstantial analogy cautiously and require cogent evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: In interpreting heroic legend as based on nature-myth, circumstantial analogy must be very cautiously appealed to, and there is need of evidence more cogent than vague likenesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid shallow analogies (e.g., 'this motif resembles that natural phenomenon') without corroborating linguistic, ritual, or distributional evidence; demand multiple lines of support before asserting nature-myth origins.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate myth from history
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics must distinguish myth from historic fact; some early writers treated myths as history in disguise (euhemerism).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a narrative is a transformed account of historical persons/events or a symbolic/natural-personalization; consider euhemerist explanations but test them against other evidence—don't assume all gods were once men nor all myths are histories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider multiple interpretative systems (plurality of methods)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different schools (allegorical, euhemerist, pragmatic, psychic, Stoic, philological, anthropological) offer divergent accounts—no single method suffices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate myths through several plausible frameworks; be wary of monocausal explanations and of applying one method dogmatically; use complementary methods when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use ethnography, popular life, and folk-rite evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: A knowledge of the popular life of antiquity is indispensable; folklorist methods (examining peasant custom and rite) reveal survivals of paganism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ground interpretations in material culture, rites, and customs; Mannhardt and later Frazer show the value of ritual and folk-practice data for reconstructing primitive meanings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish material (nature-based) myths from verbal (language-driven) myths
rubrics_metrics.description: Material myth is primary and verbal myth secondary; verbal metaphor can expand into myth in later civilization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a myth arises primarily from observable natural phenomenon and practice (material) or from the expansion of verbal/metaphorical language; this affects how heavily to weight philological explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize the limits and partial successes of each school
rubrics_metrics.description: No universal solvent for myth exists; philology yielded some secure results but many doubtful ones; similarly, solar or meteorological interpretations apply to some myths but not universally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept limited, well-supported conclusions and remain critical; test grand theories (e.g., ubiquitous sun-myths or thunder-myths) against the evidence and be ready to reject overgeneralizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use etymology as guide and safeguard (where obvious)
rubrics_metrics.description: The etymology of names is at once the guide and safeguard of the mythologist; some etymologies (e.g., Helios = sun) are obvious and useful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on clear, well-established linguistic identifications to anchor interpretations, while acknowledging they do not fully explain attendant mythic narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid rhetorical or polemical misrepresentation of opposing views
rubrics_metrics.description: Scholars should not traduce opponents or take unfair advantage of ambiguities; hypotheses need further elucidation and evidence and deserve tolerant consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain scholarly temper: require evidence-based critique rather than rhetorical dismissal; acknowledge strengths and weaknesses of other schools (author's note on Elliot Smith's school).

rubrics_metrics.name: Permit intuition as a supplement but require empirical corroboration
rubrics_metrics.description: Elucidation of myth frequently results from intuition; 'the mythologist is, like the poet, born not made,' yet intuition must be balanced by evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use scholarly intuition to generate hypotheses but seek verification via comparative, philological, ritual, or ethnographic data; do not let intuition substitute for demonstrable support (Creuzer vs. later scientific methods).
